THE INVESTMENT

Why this deserves your time.

C++ is a strong investment if robotics, autonomous vehicles, or flight software becomes your direction. It is a major language in the ROS 2 ecosystem and underpins many simulation and perception libraries. Learning it lets you understand the implementation behind a tool, extend a component, and reason about what happens when the system gets busy.

The durable skill is managing complexity without losing track of time, memory, ownership, and failure. You do not need to become a language expert before building a useful component. Progress from a small tested program to a clear interface, then to integration with other software.

Connect it to your existing tools

ROS 2, Gazebo, OpenCV, and F Prime give C++ a direct role. Arduino sketches are compiled as C++ with framework support; their simplified entry point does not represent the whole language.

FROM SYNTAX TO SYSTEMS

Problems this helps you solve.

01

Robot communication

Use ROS 2’s rclcpp client library to publish sensor information and consume commands. Message timing, queues, and missing data matter as much as the arithmetic.

02

Space software components

JPL’s F Prime is a component-driven framework with a C++ architecture. Reading its tutorials shows how commands, telemetry, and components fit into a larger system.

03

Simulation and perception

C++ powers many performance-sensitive libraries. It becomes useful when extending a simulator or processing data at a scale where measurements justify optimization.

04

Inspection machinery

A robot that handles replaceable modules needs clear states: waiting, inspecting, moving, verifying, and recovering. A desktop state-machine exercise introduces that discipline.

Evidence behind the ecosystem connections
ROS 2 client libraries ↗JPL F Prime ↗Arduino sketch build process ↗

Projects described here are learning examples. A small demonstration does not establish flight readiness or production reliability.

THE HONEST LEARNING CURVE

What is hard—and why.

C++ combines a large language with a compiler, linker, build system, and explicit resource lifetimes. Errors can appear before the program runs, or much later as memory bugs. Learning references, ownership, and debugging carefully pays off more than racing toward advanced templates.

C++ is not “C plus classes”

Modern C++ has containers, value semantics, RAII, and smart pointers. Learn std::vector and std::string before managing raw allocation yourself.

Fast is something you measure

A compiled language does not automatically make a system real-time. Scheduling, allocation, I/O, concurrency, and worst-case behavior all matter.

C is not a mandatory prerequisite

You can learn modern C++ directly after basic programming. Study C separately when embedded interfaces or coursework give it a purpose.

A trap to avoid

Do not start with template metaprogramming, custom memory allocators, or a huge robot stack. Learn the small subset needed to make one component understandable and reliable.

LEARN IN LAYERS

A sequence with a visible result.

  1. 01 · Build and debug

    Compiler messages, types, functions, const, references, std::vector and std::string.

    YOUR PROOFCompile a command-line component-mass calculator and step through it in a debugger.

  2. 02 · Make ownership clear

    Value semantics, scope, RAII, classes with a purpose, standard algorithms.

    YOUR PROOFParse a small telemetry file without unchecked indexing or manual new/delete.

  3. 03 · Organize a component

    Headers, source files, CMake basics, tests, useful diagnostics.

    YOUR PROOFModel a sensor with valid, stale, and missing states; test each transition.

  4. 04 · Integrate deliberately

    One ROS 2 publisher/subscriber or one F Prime tutorial component.

    YOUR PROOFDocument message units, expected rates, and what happens if input disappears.

Advance by understanding, not a promised number of weeks. Rebuild a small example unaided, explain an error, and check a result before adding the next layer.

A SMALL WORKING IDEA

See the reason behind the code.

TRY THE IDEA

Where did the time go?

Change the control and predict the result before looking.

Budget: one update every 20 ms. This arithmetic demo omits scheduling, jitter, I/O, and operating-system behavior. It illustrates why timing must be measured; it is not a real-time guarantee.

C++ / EXAMPLE TO STUDY
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>

int main() {
    const std::vector<double> masses_kg{1.2, 0.8, 0.5};
    double total_kg = 0.0;
    for (double mass : masses_kg) total_kg += mass;
    std::cout << total_kg << " kg\n";
}

Illustration runs in JavaScript in your browser. The C++ example is separate code to study and run in the appropriate environment.

CURATED, NOT COLLECTED

One main path. A few useful companions.

Start LearnCpp. Pair it with Programming: Principles and Practice Using C++ if you like a structured book. Use cppreference as a reference, then move to ROS 2 tutorials.

Costs checked November 4, 2026. Mixed free/paid resources can appear in both filters. Paid choices are optional; check school access and current terms before buying.

LearnCpp ↗

LearnCpp authors

A detailed, modern C++ path that includes compilation, debugging and good habits from the beginning.

How to use this resource

Work through lessons in order and compile the exercises. Learn values, functions, std::string and std::vector before advanced templates.

Free

Book · beginner

Programming: Principles and Practice Using C++, 3rd edition ↗

Bjarne Stroustrup / Addison-Wesley

A programming foundation by C++’s creator, using contemporary C++20/23.

How to use this resource

Choose this as a book-based alternative to LearnCpp. Do the drills, and check the book’s setup guidance for its support library.

Paid book; companion material free

Reference · reference

C++ reference ↗

cppreference community

A detailed lookup for language rules, standard containers and library behavior.

How to use this resource

Look up one function at a time; pay attention to the C++ standard version. This is a reference, not a first course.

Free

Engineering guidelines · next

C++ Core Guidelines ↗

Bjarne Stroustrup, Herb Sutter and contributors

Explains resource ownership, interfaces and maintainability—the issues that matter as robotics code grows.

How to use this resource

After basic classes, focus on resource management, const correctness and interfaces. Apply one rule to a small project each week.

Free

Build-system tutorial · next

CMake Tutorial ↗

Kitware / CMake

Teaches how to build and link projects that contain multiple source files and libraries.

How to use this resource

Use after you can compile a small C++ program. Create a reusable library plus a small executable before entering a ROS workspace.

Free

Robotics tutorials · next

ROS 2 Jazzy tutorials ↗

ROS 2 project / Open Robotics contributors

Applies C++ to nodes, topics, services and robot-software communication.

How to use this resource

Use documentation matching your installed ROS distribution. Start with command-line tools, then a C++ publisher/subscriber; do not start here to learn basic C++ syntax.

THE NEXT SMALL WIN

Compile a program that stores three component masses in std::vector<double> and prints their sum. Change one value, predict the output, then use the debugger to inspect the loop.

A useful session ends with evidence

  1. Predict. What should happen, and why?
  2. Write. Spend most of the time in code.
  3. Check. Try a simple value and an awkward one.
  4. Explain. Describe the result in your own words.

Use AI for hints, explanations, and review. Attempt the task first, follow course rules, and finish by solving a small variant unaided.

EVIDENCE OF PROGRESS

Could you do it without a walkthrough?

A PROJECT WORTH KEEPING

Build a simulated inspection supervisor. Feed it prerecorded sensor messages and make it choose between “continue inspection,” “request review,” and “missing input.” Add tests before attaching a physical robot.

Save the code, sample input, a short README, assumptions and units, a test case, and a result you can explain. That is stronger evidence than a completed playlist.
